transcript.text: Beko vented dryer, drum goes round fine but it's just blowing cold air. Had it about 6 years. What part do I need?

The most likely culprit is the heating element assembly or one of the thermostats/thermal cut-outs attached to it. On most Beko vented dryers, these come as a single part (element + thermostats), so that's often what people end up buying.

## Most likely causes (in order)

1. Thermal cut-out (TCO) tripped or blown. This is a safety device that cuts the heat if the dryer overheats. On many Beko models it's a one-time fuse, and it can't be reset. It usually blows because of poor airflow.
2. Heating element broken. The coil goes open-circuit with age. This is very common at around 6 years.
3. Cycling thermostat failed. This is less common but possible.
4. Timer or control board fault. This is rare. Rule out everything above first.

## Before you buy anything

• Check the obvious. Make sure it's not on a "cool," "air dry," or low-heat setting.
• Check airflow. Clean the lint filter properly. Check the vent hose for kinks, crushing, or a build-up of fluff, and make sure the outside flap opens freely. If airflow is restricted, a new part will just blow again. This is the number one reason TCOs fail.

## Testing (if you have a multimeter)

Unplug the dryer first. The element is usually behind the back panel. With the wires disconnected, test each part:

• Heating element: It should read roughly 20–30 ohms. An open circuit or infinite reading means it's broken.
• Thermostats/TCO: At room temperature, they should read close to 0 ohms. An open circuit means it's faulty.

## Getting the right part

Find the model number. It's on a sticker inside the door rim or on the back, and looks something like DRVS62W or DCV83. Search "[model number] heater element" on a parts site such as eSpares, Partmaster, or Beko's own spares shop. The full element assembly with thermostats usually costs £20–£40 and is a fairly simple DIY job with a screwdriver.

If you send me the model number, I can help you narrow down the exact part.

It says DV7110 on the front, but the label's on the back and the dryer is wedged in a tight alcove so I can't read the rest. I cleaned the lint filter, which was fairly full, and the vent hose was badly clogged with fluff, so I cleaned that out too. Airflow at the hose end is decent now, but it's still cold after 20 mins. It's cold on both high and low heat, and I've got no multimeter. Which part do I order?

## What's most likely wrong

A badly clogged vent hose plus no heat on any setting strongly suggests a blown thermal cut-out (TCO). Restricted airflow makes the dryer overheat, and the TCO does its job by cutting the heat. On most Beko vented models it's a one-time fuse, so clearing the hose won't bring the heat back. It needs replacing.

## What to order (no multimeter)

Order the complete heater element assembly with thermostats/TCO already fitted. That covers the TCO, the element, and the cycling thermostat in one part, so it fixes all three of the most likely causes. It costs a bit more than the TCO alone, but you avoid guessing and having to pull the dryer out twice.

Search "Beko DV7110 heater element" on eSpares, Partmaster, or Beko's spares site. Colour variants (DV7110W, DV7110S, etc.) usually take the same part, but most sites let you enter the full model number to confirm.

## Before you click buy

You'll have to pull the dryer out of the alcove anyway, because the element is behind the back panel. So:

1. Unplug it and pull it out.
2. Read the full model number on the rear label and check it against the part listing.
3. Take the back panel off and look. A snapped coil on the element is sometimes visible, and you'll see whether the thermostats are separate parts or built into the element assembly.

## Optional: cheaper route

A basic multimeter costs about £10–15. If the element tests fine and only the TCO is open-circuit, a thermostat/TCO kit is often under £15, which saves you replacing a good element. It's worth it if you like DIY. If not, the full assembly is the safe bet.

## Afterwards

Keep the vent hose short and as straight as possible, and clear the fluff from it every few months. Otherwise the new TCO will blow the same way.
